intro: Cart abandonment rate is the share of started carts or checkouts that never turned into a completed purchase. Enter carts started and completed purchases to get the rate.

sections.heading: How Cart Abandonment Rate is calculated
sections.body: Abandonment Rate = (Carts started − Completed purchases) ÷ Carts started — [the same started-minus-completed-over-started shape AgencyAnalytics uses to define cart abandonment rate](https://agencyanalytics.com/kpi-definitions/cart-abandonment-rate/). The stage matters as much as the formula: this calculator can measure abandonment at the cart stage or the checkout stage, and the two describe different points in the funnel — a lower checkout-stage abandonment rate doesn't mean fewer people abandoned overall, since anyone who never reached checkout was already excluded from that denominator.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.body: (1,000 − 280) ÷ 1,000 = 72.00%. This is a cart-stage number specifically — it counts everyone who started a cart, including people who never made it to checkout at all. A checkout-stage figure computed on the same traffic would answer a narrower question and produce a different rate. Whether those 720 abandoned carts are worth chasing depends on what a recovered one is likely to be worth, which is what [AOV](/calculators/aov) measures for the same traffic.

sections.heading: Cart-stage vs. checkout-stage abandonment aren't the same number
sections.body: Cart-stage abandonment counts every started cart, whether or not that visitor ever reached checkout. Checkout-stage abandonment counts only carts that reached checkout, which is a smaller, further-qualified group. A site can have a high cart-stage abandonment rate (lots of casual cart adds that never go anywhere) alongside a much lower checkout-stage rate (of the people who got that far, most finished) — both numbers can be true at once and aren't contradicting each other. There's also a measurement-layer version of this ambiguity: [some analytics setups count "add to cart" as an event, which can fire more than once per visitor, rather than as a distinct cart](https://agencyanalytics.com/kpi-definitions/cart-abandonment-rate/) — a cart abandonment rate built on event counts and one built on deduplicated carts can disagree even when nothing about actual shopper behavior changed.

sections.heading: Cart Abandonment Rate vs. Conversion Rate
sections.body: These look like mirror images of each other, but their denominators cover different populations. [Conversion Rate](/calculators/cr) divides completed purchases by total visitors — everyone who showed up to the site, whether they ever added anything to a cart or not. Cart Abandonment Rate divides the shortfall by carts started specifically, a narrower group that's already shown some purchase intent. A site can improve its cart abandonment rate by fixing checkout friction while its overall conversion rate barely moves, if the bigger drop-off is happening earlier, before a cart is ever started.

sections.heading: Common mistakes
items: Comparing a cart-stage abandonment rate against a checkout-stage figure as if they measure the same thing. They cover different populations, and a gap between the two doesn't mean one number is wrong.

Treating "add to cart" events as the same thing as distinct carts. Some analytics setups count the event every time it fires, which can inflate the denominator relative to how many actual shopping sessions started a cart.
Reading a rising abandonment rate as automatically bad without checking whether more low-intent traffic (e.g. from a new acquisition channel) is now reaching the cart stage in the first place.

Comparing abandonment rate across devices or traffic sources without accounting for it. Mobile checkout friction, payment method availability, and session length can all shift the rate for reasons unrelated to the underlying offer.

faq.a: Cart abandonment rate is the percentage of started carts or checkouts that never turned into a completed purchase, calculated as (carts started minus completed purchases) divided by carts started. It's a funnel-stage metric, not a whole-site conversion metric: the denominator is only the people who already showed some purchase intent by starting a cart, not every visitor to the site. This calculator can measure the rate at either the cart stage or the checkout stage, and the two aren't interchangeable — a cart-stage rate includes everyone who added something to a cart, while a checkout-stage rate only covers the narrower group that reached checkout before abandoning.

faq.q: How do you calculate Cart Abandonment Rate?
faq.a: Subtract completed purchases from carts started, then divide by carts started: Abandonment Rate = (Carts started − Completed purchases) ÷ Carts started. A site with 1,000 carts started and 280 completed purchases has an abandonment rate of (1,000 − 280) ÷ 1,000 = 72.00%. Both numbers need to describe the same stage and the same time period — mixing a cart-stage count with a checkout-stage count, or comparing figures from different date ranges, produces a rate that doesn't accurately describe either. The stage being measured (cart or checkout) should always be stated alongside the result, since the two describe different populations.

faq.q: Is cart-stage abandonment the same as checkout-stage abandonment?
faq.a: No. Cart-stage abandonment counts every visitor who started a cart, including many who never got close to paying. Checkout-stage abandonment only counts visitors who reached checkout — a smaller, further-qualified group that had already cleared the earlier funnel steps. A site can have a high cart-stage rate driven by casual browsers adding items with no real intent to buy, alongside a much lower checkout-stage rate among the people who actually got that far. Neither number is more "correct" than the other; they answer different questions about different stages of the same funnel, and should be reported with the stage explicitly named.

faq.q: How is Cart Abandonment Rate different from Conversion Rate?
faq.a: Conversion Rate divides completed purchases by every visitor to the site, regardless of whether they ever added anything to a cart. Cart Abandonment Rate divides the shortfall between carts started and completed purchases by carts started specifically — a narrower population that already showed purchase intent. A site can improve its cart abandonment rate significantly by streamlining checkout, while its overall conversion rate stays flat if most of the drop-off is actually happening earlier, before anyone starts a cart at all. The two metrics are diagnosing different parts of the same funnel, not competing measurements of one underlying thing, which is why a strong move in one doesn't guarantee the other follows.

faq.q: What is a good Cart Abandonment Rate?
faq.a: There's no single good abandonment rate that applies everywhere — it varies by industry, device mix, price point, and whether the number is measured at the cart or checkout stage, all of which shift the rate before checkout quality even enters the picture. A high-consideration purchase naturally sees more cart adds that never convert than an impulse-buy category does, and mobile traffic typically abandons at a different rate than desktop for reasons unrelated to the checkout experience itself. The more useful comparison is your own site's rate over time, at a consistent stage and traffic mix, rather than an external number that has no visibility into what's actually being sold.

qaNotes:
STANDARD depth (Batch 06). Formula/example independently verified: (1000-280)/1000=0.72=72.00%, matches calculator-catalog.json's exampleOutput exactly. Metric-specific section (cart-vs-checkout-stage) built directly from this calculator's own documented validationRule ('the stage label must be shown in the result, since cart-stage and checkout-stage numbers are not comparable to each other') plus a genuine measurement-layer nuance (add-to-cart as an event vs a distinct cart) sourced from AgencyAnalytics. Comparison-note (Cart Abandonment vs Conversion Rate) via numerator/denominator/business-question framing - no cannibalization risk flagged in calculator-seo-map.json but a natural, foreseeable confusion given both are funnel-stage percentages. No unsupported benchmark - good-abandonment-rate FAQ names the actual variables (industry, device mix, price point, stage) rather than citing the commonly-quoted ~70% aggregate average (deliberately not used - that figure describes an industry-wide blended statistic, not a target any individual site should aim for, and using it risked exactly the 'good X = Y%' benchmark this batch's policy prohibits). External source: AgencyAnalytics' own Cart Abandonment Rate KPI definition page (same started-minus-completed-over-started formula this calculator implements, and the explicit cart-vs-checkout distinction). 2 contextual internal links: /calculators/cr (comparison-note) and /calculators/aov (worked-example, what a recovered cart is worth). Related Calculators verified live: cr, revenue-per-visitor, aov (catalog's own relatedCalculators list for this slug - cr, bounce-rate-landing - has only one live entry, so cr plus two additional genuinely relevant live calculators were used instead). 5 FAQs, 100-150 words each, independently word-counted.

PRODUCTION ROUND (formula/edge-case audit): added a scoped cross-field check to calc-validate.ts rejecting completedPurchases > cartsCreated (the calculator's own documented validationRule), and a catalog-driven strictlyPositive check rejecting cartsCreated = 0 (was previously accepted per-field, silently producing a bare '-' result with no field-level error - see calc-catalog.ts's withPositivity for the generic, corpus-wide fix). Both verified live: purchases>carts now shows 'Can't exceed carts created'; cartsCreated=0 now shows 'Must be greater than zero'; the canonical 1,000/280->72.00% example and this round's own example (1,000/300->70.00%) both still compute correctly.
